group.passage:
Have you ever seen something that looks like a human face in an unexpected place? When you casually walk down the street and look up at the clouds in the sky, you will be surprised to discover the face of Jesus Christ up there. Is it the Resurrection you happen to witness? No way! In fact, it is because of a phenomenon called pareidolia [[1]] you are misled. Its occurrence is due to our brain’s tendency to organize unclear images into something we find meaningful.
According to scientists, human beings possess the innate ability to recognize faces. Therefore, it is normal for us to perceive them in objects. However, pareidolia is not [[2]] face recognition. It can also lead us to spot items or animals we are familiar with almost everywhere. For example, with just a quick glance, we are likely to find a flying dragon on a rugged rock. It is truly amazing that our brain should be capable of swiftly making connections and giving new definitions to [[3]] patterns we encounter.
A classic example of pareidolia is the shaping of constellations, or star signs. [[4]], pareidolia sheds light on the reason why ancient astronomers connected the dots and conceived the patterns we make sense of. After all, it does not take a great deal of imagination to see a lion in Leo, a scorpion in Scorpius, or a mighty hunter in Orion. Based on the examples mentioned above, it [[5]] us that seeing is not always believing. What we see may be nothing but a surrealistic work by our brain.

tags.topic: pareidolia: seeing faces and patterns in random objects
